title: Zero Trust architecture for endpoints
summary: Apply the Zero Trust model to endpoints, treating device identity, health and signal as first-class inputs to every access decision. You will map the Microsoft Zero Trust pillars to concrete endpoint controls you can deploy today.
objectives: Explain the three Zero Trust principles and why implicit trust by network location is obsolete
Map the Zero Trust pillars to endpoint controls: identity, device, app, data, network
Describe how device compliance state becomes a signal in an access decision
Differentiate authentication, authorization and continuous access evaluation at the endpoint
Design a high-level Zero Trust enforcement flow for a managed Windows device
Identify the telemetry sources that feed endpoint trust decisions

quiz.q: Which statement best captures the core assumption of Zero Trust?
options: Devices inside the corporate network are trusted by default
Assume breach and verify every request explicitly regardless of network location
VPN-connected devices need no further checks
Trust is granted once at logon and never re-evaluated
quiz.why: Zero Trust replaces the perimeter model with explicit, per-request verification under an assume-breach posture, so network location alone never confers trust.

quiz.q: In a Zero Trust access decision for an endpoint, which is treated as a primary signal alongside user identity?
options: The device's compliance and health state
The colour of the desktop wallpaper
quiz.why: Device compliance and health (managed, encrypted, patched, not flagged by EDR) are first-class signals that Conditional Access and the access broker evaluate before granting access.

quiz.q: What does the principle of 'least privilege' add to endpoint Zero Trust?
options: It grants admin rights to all users for convenience
It limits access with just-in-time and just-enough-access and risk-based adaptive policies
It disables all auditing to reduce noise
It removes the need for MFA
quiz.why: Least privilege means scoping access tightly using JIT/JEA and adaptive, risk-based policies so a compromised endpoint or account has minimal blast radius.

quiz.q: Why is Continuous Access Evaluation (CAE) important in a Zero Trust endpoint design?
options: It caches tokens forever to improve speed
It lets revocation and risk changes take effect near real time instead of waiting for token expiry
It replaces the need for device compliance
quiz.why: CAE allows critical events such as account disable, password reset or elevated risk to revoke access in near real time rather than waiting up to an hour for token lifetime to lapse.

quiz.q: Name the five core Microsoft Zero Trust pillars that an endpoint design touches.
quiz.answer: Identity, Devices (endpoints), Applications, Data, and Network (with Infrastructure often added as a sixth).
quiz.why: Microsoft's Zero Trust model spans Identity, Endpoints/Devices, Apps, Data, Network and Infrastructure; an endpoint strategy must consider how the device interacts with each.

quiz.q: In one sentence, explain why 'assume breach' changes how you design endpoint controls.
quiz.answer: Because you design as though an attacker is already present, you segment access, verify continuously, encrypt data and minimise privilege so a single compromised endpoint cannot move laterally or exfiltrate freely.
quiz.why: Assume breach shifts focus from keeping attackers out to limiting damage, driving micro-segmentation, least privilege, encryption and rich telemetry on every endpoint.

body_markdown:
## The perimeter is gone

For decades security assumed a hard shell and a soft centre: get past the firewall or onto the VPN, and you were trusted. Cloud apps, remote work and BYOD destroyed that model. **Zero Trust** replaces it with three principles: **verify explicitly**, use **least-privilege access**, and **assume breach**. Network location is no longer a trust signal. Every request — including from a device sitting in your own office — must be authenticated, authorized and validated against current signals.

For an endpoint engineer this is a mindset shift. The device stops being a passive client and becomes an active participant whose **health and compliance state** feed directly into whether access is granted.

## The pillars and how endpoints touch each

Microsoft's Zero Trust model spans **Identity, Devices, Applications, Data, Network** and Infrastructure. An endpoint sits at the intersection:

- **Identity** — the user and the device both have identities (the device identity comes from Entra join or hybrid join).
- **Devices** — compliance policy decides if the endpoint is healthy: encrypted, patched, EDR-onboarded, not jailbroken.
- **Applications** — app protection policies and managed app access.
- **Data** — encryption at rest (BitLocker) and labelling/DLP in transit.
- **Network** — segmentation so a compromised endpoint cannot roam.

## Compliance state as a signal

The heart of endpoint Zero Trust is that **device compliance becomes an input to authorization**. Intune evaluates a device against policy and stamps it compliant or non-compliant. **Conditional Access** then consumes that state. A simplified decision flow looks like this:

```text
User + device request access to resource
  -> Authenticate user (MFA / passwordless)
  -> Evaluate signals: user risk, sign-in risk, device compliance, location, app
  -> Decision: Grant / Grant with controls / Block
  -> Continuously re-evaluate (CAE) for revocation & risk change
```

Notice authorization is **not** a one-time gate. With **Continuous Access Evaluation (CAE)** a disabled account, a password reset or a sudden risk spike can revoke a live session in near real time, instead of waiting for a token to expire.

## Least privilege at the endpoint

Assume breach means scoping access tightly. On the endpoint that translates to removing standing local-admin rights, using **just-in-time** elevation, and applying **just-enough-access**. You can confirm a user is not a standing admin:

```powershell
# List members of the local Administrators group
Get-LocalGroupMember -Group 'Administrators' |
  Select-Object Name, PrincipalSource, ObjectClass
```

Every account that does not strictly need elevation is removed. A compromised standard user is far less useful to an attacker than a compromised admin.

## Telemetry feeds the decision

Zero Trust only works if the signals are trustworthy and current. Endpoint telemetry — sign-in logs, **Defender for Endpoint** alerts, Intune compliance, and device risk scores — flows into the policy engine. The richer and fresher the signal, the better the decision. This is why EDR onboarding and compliance reporting are not optional extras; they are the sensory system of your access control.

## Your task

For one managed Windows device in a test tenant, document its full Zero Trust posture: device join type, compliance policy result, BitLocker and EDR onboarding state, and the local Administrators membership. Then draw the access-decision flow for that device reaching a sensitive app, naming every signal Conditional Access would evaluate and where CAE would intervene on a revocation event.

slides.title: Zero Trust architecture for endpoints
slides.sub: Month 3 - Advanced Endpoint Security & Identity  |  Lesson 1
slides.narration: Welcome to Month Three, where we move from supporting endpoints to securing and hardening them. This first lesson is about the model that underpins everything else we'll do: Zero Trust. By the end you'll understand the three principles, how the Microsoft pillars map onto endpoint controls, and why your device's health is now part of every access decision.

slides.title: The perimeter is gone
bullets: The old model trusted anything past the firewall or VPN.
Cloud, remote work and BYOD broke that assumption.
Network location is no longer a trust signal.
Every request must be verified, wherever it comes from.
slides.narration: Let's start with why we even need this. For decades, security assumed a hard outer shell and a soft trusted centre. Get past the firewall or onto the V P N and you were trusted. But cloud apps, remote work and bring your own device demolished that. Today a request from a laptop in your own office is treated with exactly the same suspicion as one from a coffee shop. Location tells us nothing about trust anymore.

slides.title: Three principles
bullets: Verify explicitly — authenticate and authorize every request.
Least privilege — just-in-time and just-enough-access.
Assume breach — design as if the attacker is already in.
These three ideas drive every control we build.
slides.narration: Zero Trust rests on three principles. Verify explicitly: authenticate and authorize every single request using all available signals. Use least privilege: grant the minimum access needed, just in time, just enough. And assume breach: design as though an attacker is already inside your environment. Hold these three in your head, because every control in this month is a direct expression of one of them.

slides.title: The pillars and the endpoint
bullets: Identity, Devices, Apps, Data, Network, Infrastructure.
The endpoint sits at the intersection of all of them.
The device itself has an identity from Entra join.
Compliance state ties the device into authorization.
slides.narration: Microsoft frames Zero Trust across pillars: identity, devices, applications, data, network and infrastructure. As an endpoint engineer, your device sits right at the intersection. The user has an identity, but so does the device, from Entra join or hybrid join. And critically, the device's compliance state becomes part of the authorization decision. The endpoint is no longer a passive client; it's an active participant in trust.

slides.title: Compliance as a signal
bullets: Intune evaluates the device against compliance policy.
It stamps the device compliant or non-compliant.
Conditional Access consumes that state in its decision.
Healthy means encrypted, patched, EDR-onboarded.
slides.narration: Here's the mechanism at the heart of it. Intune evaluates each device against a compliance policy and stamps it compliant or non-compliant. Conditional Access then consumes that stamp as a signal. A healthy device is encrypted, patched, onboarded to E D R and not flagged as at risk. If the device falls out of compliance, access to sensitive resources can be cut. The device's health is now load-bearing.

slides.title: The decision flow
bullets: Authenticate the user, ideally passwordless.
Evaluate signals: risk, compliance, location, app.
Decide: grant, grant with controls, or block.
Re-evaluate continuously — not a one-time gate.
slides.code:
User + device request access
  -> Authenticate user (MFA / passwordless)
  -> Evaluate: user risk, sign-in risk,
     device compliance, location, app
  -> Decision: Grant / Grant + controls / Block
  -> Continuously re-evaluate (CAE)
slides.narration: Let's trace a request. The user and device ask for a resource. First we authenticate the user, ideally passwordless. Then we evaluate the signals: user risk, sign-in risk, device compliance, location, the app being accessed. From that we decide: grant, grant with extra controls like a fresh M F A prompt, or block outright. And crucially this isn't a one-time gate at logon — we keep re-evaluating.

slides.title: Continuous Access Evaluation
bullets: Tokens normally live up to an hour before re-check.
CAE lets critical events revoke access in near real time.
Account disable, password reset, risk spike all trigger it.
Authorization becomes continuous, not a single moment.
slides.narration: That continuous part matters. Normally an access token is valid for up to an hour, so revoking access could take that long to bite. Continuous Access Evaluation changes that. When a critical event happens — an account is disabled, a password is reset, risk suddenly spikes — the resource is told to revoke the live session in near real time. Authorization stops being a single moment at logon and becomes an ongoing conversation.

slides.title: Least privilege on the device
bullets: Remove standing local-admin rights from users.
Use just-in-time elevation when admin is truly needed.
A compromised standard user has a small blast radius.
Audit who sits in the local Administrators group.
slides.narration: Assume breach pushes us to least privilege right on the endpoint. That means stripping standing local-admin rights from everyday users and granting elevation just in time when it's genuinely needed. Why? Because a compromised standard user is far less useful to an attacker than a compromised admin — the blast radius is tiny. Start by auditing who actually sits in the local Administrators group with this command, then trim it ruthlessly.

slides.title: Telemetry is the nervous system
bullets: Sign-in logs, Defender alerts, compliance, risk scores.
Signals must be trustworthy and current to be useful.
EDR onboarding and compliance reporting aren't optional.
Fresh, rich signal equals better access decisions.
slides.narration: None of this works without good signal. Zero Trust decisions are only as good as the telemetry feeding them: sign-in logs, Defender for Endpoint alerts, Intune compliance, device risk scores. That's why onboarding every endpoint to E D R and getting compliance reporting clean aren't nice-to-haves; they're the nervous system of your access control. Fresh, rich, trustworthy signal produces good decisions. Stale or missing signal produces bad ones.

slides.title: Recap & your task
bullets: Verify explicitly, least privilege, assume breach.
Device compliance is a first-class access signal.
CAE makes authorization continuous, not one-time.
Task: document one device's full Zero Trust posture.
slides.narration: Let's recap. Zero Trust means verify explicitly, grant least privilege, and assume breach. The device's compliance state is now a first-class signal in every access decision, and Continuous Access Evaluation makes that authorization continuous rather than a single gate at logon. Your task: pick one managed Windows device in a test tenant and document its full Zero Trust posture — join type, compliance result, BitLocker and E D R state, and local admin membership. Then draw the access-decision flow for that device reaching a sensitive app, naming every signal Conditional Access would weigh and where C A E would step in on revocation. See you in the next lesson.
